newsitem.title: UK: Harrods in court bid to protect name.
newsitem.headline: Harrods in court bid to protect name.

text.p: Top-class department store Harrods launched a High Court bid on Tuesday to block moves to sell off its world famous name to the highest bidder.

The London store is challenging the right of Harrods (Buenos Aires) Ltd and its associate company Harrods (South America) to cash in on an 80-year-old agreement, entitling them to use the name, by selling off the right to use it world wide.

"Were the defendants to be free to sell the name throughout the rest of the world, the result...could mean the name Harrods would come to mean nothing. Harrods would be just a word in common parlance," Charles Sparrow, lawyer for Harrods, told the court.
"The name Harrods would no longer mean, and mean only, that very special store in Knightsbridge, London," Sparrow said.
Harrods, now owned by Egyptian-born Mohammed al-Fayed, was established in 1849 and has more than 12 million customers worldwide, he said.
Sparrow said Harrods (Buenos Aires) was established at the turn of the century with the aim of running a store by the same name in then wealthy Argentina.
In the late 1960s, Harrods sold their shares in Harrods (Buenos Aires) but allowed the company to continue using the name.
But the downturn in the Argentinian economy caused financial problems for the Buenos Aires company and it was trying to salvage its position by selling the name, Sparrow said.
Harrods was alerted by a 1994 circular issued by the Buenos Aires company seeking investment.
Sparrow said the high reputation of the London store worldwide would be lost if the South American company was allowed to go ahead with plans to market the Harrods name internationally.
"They are going to buy it to use it and the name would be destroyed," he told the court.
The hearing is expected to last two weeks.
